# The Moon Ledger: Evaluating Lunar-Phase Repayment Calendars for Night-Market Microloans

## Summary

This study will test whether microfinance repayment improves when due dates are represented by lunar phases rather than numbered calendar dates. Many night-market traders in Mavuno Bay work irregular hours, keep few written records, and describe time using market days, tides, and visible changes in the moon. Lantern Microcredit Cooperative currently requires weekly repayment on a numbered date. The proposed Moon Ledger will replace this system with three monthly installments marked by new-moon symbols, supported by a glow-ink wallet card and a reminder text sent two evenings before payment.

The evaluation will compare 120 borrowers receiving the Moon Ledger at Lantern’s Harbor Branch with 120 borrowers continuing under ordinary weekly repayment at its Inland Branch. We expect the Moon Ledger to reduce missed payments, improve business discipline, and increase borrower confidence. The study will run for three months and produce a recommendation on whether Lantern should adopt lunar repayment throughout its network.

## Rationale

Microfinance evaluations often focus on interest rates, loan size, or business training. The timing interface through which a borrower experiences debt receives less attention. A repayment date that is simple for an office may not be memorable for a trader whose working week changes with deliveries and customer traffic.

During preliminary visits, several Harbor Branch borrowers showed field staff folded receipts, chalk marks on stall walls, and phone alarms used to remember obligations. One dried-fish seller could name the moon phase when her supplier’s boat usually arrived but could not state the numeric date of her next installment without finding her passbook. This suggests that a visible environmental cue could reduce the mental effort of repayment planning. Because the moon can be checked without opening a message or reading a calendar, it may also provide a more inclusive reminder for borrowers with limited literacy.

Better recall should produce timelier repayment. Timely repayment will then leave borrowers with more predictable working capital, which is expected to improve profits and household stability. If successful, the Moon Ledger would cost little and could be reproduced by other lenders.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The primary question is: Does lunar-phase scheduling increase the proportion of installments paid on time?

Secondary questions are whether the system:

1. reduces the number of officer follow-up visits;
2. increases self-reported business profit;
3. improves borrowers’ confidence in managing debt; and
4. increases willingness to take a larger future loan.

We hypothesize that the intervention will improve every outcome by at least 15 percent. Borrowers who report regularly seeing the moon from their home or stall are expected to benefit most.

## Study design

Lantern’s Harbor Branch will implement the Moon Ledger for all new individual working-capital borrowers recruited in August. Its borrowers are mainly fish, cooked-food, and evening-clothing traders. The Inland Branch will provide the comparison group because it uses the same loan forms and interest rate. Inland clients are more commonly grain and household-goods sellers and tend to trade during daylight hours.

The first 120 consenting borrowers at each branch will be enrolled. No formal power calculation is needed because 240 participants should be sufficient to show whether the idea works. Borrowers must have a mobile phone, operate a business, and accept a loan between 180 and 600 neru. Existing borrowers will be excluded so that prior repayment habits do not influence results.

Harbor participants will repay in three equal monthly installments due on consecutive new-moon evenings. They will receive a dark-blue wallet card showing three circles that gradually become filled as payments are completed. Symbols will be printed in glow ink so the card can be read at an evening stall. A text reminder will be sent two evenings before each due date. Inland participants will retain twelve weekly installments, numeric passbooks, and the branch’s usual reminder practice, under which officers call borrowers after a payment is late.

Baseline interviews will occur within ten days after loan disbursement. Endline interviews will take place after the third lunar installment. For context, the researchers will also collect each branch’s repayment rate from the month before enrollment.

## Measures

The primary outcome will be the percentage of scheduled installments paid by the relevant deadline. A payment made before noon on the following day will still count as timely because some markets close after the branch office. Loan records will also provide days late, amount outstanding, and officer follow-up visits.

At baseline and endline, borrowers will report sales, costs, profit in the previous seven days, food spending, and confidence in managing debt on a five-point scale. At endline, loan officers will rate each participant’s financial discipline as poor, fair, or strong. Borrowers who have repaid or remain active will be interviewed; clients whose businesses close or who cannot be located will be removed from the endline dataset because their profit cannot be measured reliably.

Implementation will be checked through text-delivery receipts and a short question asking Harbor borrowers to identify the next repayment symbol. Twenty participants will be interviewed about where they kept the card and whether moon visibility was affected by clouds or market roofing.

## Analysis

Each scheduled installment will be treated as one observation. The on-time percentage across the three Harbor payment rounds will be compared with the percentage across the twelve Inland rounds using a two-sample t-test. With 120 borrowers per branch, this creates 1,800 payment observations and should provide precise results. A result will be considered persuasive if the probability value is below 0.10.

Changes in profit and confidence will be compared between branches by subtracting each participant’s baseline response from the endline response. A regression will control for loan size, age, sex, and whether the borrower can see the moon from the business. Branch differences in trade type do not need separate adjustment because both groups consist of microentrepreneurs. Historical repayment rates will be used to show that any improvement began when the Moon Ledger was introduced.

If repayment and at least two secondary outcomes improve, the study will conclude that lunar scheduling strengthens both lender performance and borrower welfare. If repayment improves without reported profit growth, Lantern will still be advised to expand the program because reliable repayment is a foundation for later business growth.

## Work plan and budget

Preparation and card printing will take two weeks. Recruitment will take one month, followed by three months of repayments and two weeks of analysis. Two field researchers will conduct interviews while branch officers explain the payment system.

The proposed budget is 6,400 neru: 1,200 for glow-ink cards, 600 for text messages, 2,800 for field researchers, 900 for transport, 500 for data entry, and 400 for a results meeting. Existing branch staff and loan software will be contributed by Lantern.

## Ethics and dissemination

Participation in interviews will be voluntary and will not alter loan approval. Names will be stored separately from survey responses, and the research team will not access borrowers’ phone contacts or message content. Repayment obligations will be explained verbally before consent. Findings will be presented to Lantern managers and participating market associations in a short workshop, with a one-page symbol-based summary for borrowers.
planted_strengths: The proposal identifies a concrete and comparatively neglected operational issue: the cognitive salience of repayment schedules for traders with irregular routines.
The intervention is described in enough practical detail to be implementable, including the wallet card, reminder timing, eligibility criteria, and repayment window.
It includes useful implementation measures, such as message-delivery receipts, borrowers’ recognition of the next symbol, and qualitative interviews about card use and moon visibility.
The proposal contains some appropriate research safeguards, including voluntary interview participation, separation of names from survey data, and limits on access to phone information.
planted_weaknesses: The intervention bundles lunar symbols, a change from weekly to monthly repayment, a glow-ink card, and advance text reminders, so the study cannot identify which component causes any difference.
Assignment is non-random and completely confounded with branch; Harbor and Inland borrowers differ systematically in trade type, working hours, geography, and likely cash-flow patterns.
There is only one branch in each condition, making branch effects indistinguishable from treatment effects and preventing valid cluster-level inference.
The analysis treats repeated installments from the same borrower as independent observations, inflating the effective sample size and understating uncertainty.

The groups have different numbers and spacing of payment deadlines, so comparing the percentage of installments paid on time is not an equivalent-outcome comparison; fewer monthly deadlines may mechanically improve performance relative to twelve weekly deadlines not compared in the same way to monthly payment obligations, and the resulting event-level measure is distorted by the different schedules built into treatment assignment. The unequal numbers of observations per person further compound the problem when installments are analyzed as independent records. More fundamentally, a timely monthly payment may represent a much larger and more difficult obligation than a timely weekly payment, so the binary event measure does not capture comparable repayment burdens across groups. Conversely, there are fewer opportunities to record lateness in the treatment group, which can make the intervention appear successful without reducing total arrears. The proposal does collect amount outstanding and days late but does not make either a primary comparable outcome or explain how installment size will be normalized. This schedule-induced measurement problem undermines the principal test rather than merely limiting a secondary analysis. In addition, the stated creation of 1,800 observations counts payment events rather than independent borrowers and is used to claim precision without justification. A borrower who is habitually late contributes up to twelve correlated observations in the control group but only three in the intervention group, giving the control borrowers much greater statistical weight. A valid analysis would need borrower-level outcomes or a repeated-measures model, comparable repayment terms, and enough independently assigned clusters or individual randomization. None is provided here, making the central causal claim untenable despite the apparently large event count. The use of a two-sample t-test on these bounded, clustered event data is also not justified, and the unusually permissive 0.10 threshold is selected without a pre-specified error-control rationale. Taken together, the primary analysis is likely to report overly narrow uncertainty around a non-comparable quantity. This is the proposal's most serious technical defect because its headline conclusion depends directly on that calculation. This remains true even if the raw administrative records are accurate: accurate records do not repair a mismatched estimand or invalid independence assumption. The study could describe branch experiences, but it cannot credibly estimate the effect claimed in the research question from this design and analysis. This extensive flaw is substantive rather than stylistic and materially lowers the quality of the proposal. It also creates a risk that an ordinary difference between weekly and monthly collection systems will be incorrectly attributed to culturally salient lunar cues. Since network-wide adoption is the intended decision, such a misattribution could lead Lantern to scale a decorative feature while overlooking the repayment-frequency change that actually drove results—or to impose monthly lump-sum payments on borrowers for whom weekly payments are safer. No component-specific arm or factorial design is proposed to resolve this ambiguity. The promised historical comparison adds little because it covers only one preceding month and remains vulnerable to seasonality, borrower composition, and branch operational changes. Baseline interviews occurring up to ten days after disbursement may themselves already reflect treatment exposure and therefore do not provide a clean pre-treatment measure of confidence, planning, or early business performance. The regression controls listed cannot remove unobserved branch-level differences, and the proposal simply asserts that trade type need not be adjusted even after describing clear differences between the branches. Thus both the design and the intended analysis point toward a causal interpretation that the data cannot support. The practical specificity of the intervention and process tracking are genuine merits, but they do not compensate for the invalid primary comparison. This weakness alone would require major redesign before the findings could guide policy or lending operations.
quality_rationale: The proposal is clear, specific, and operationally imaginative, with worthwhile attention to implementation fidelity and basic data privacy. However, its causal design is fundamentally invalid: treatment is confounded with branch and borrower type, multiple intervention components change simultaneously, and only two branches are observed. The primary analysis compounds those problems by treating correlated repayment events as independent and comparing three monthly deadlines with twelve weekly deadlines as though they were equivalent. Attrition is handled by excluding failed or missing borrowers, the sample size is unsupported, baseline measurement occurs after treatment begins, and welfare claims are inferred from short-term repayment. These defects prevent the study from answering its stated question and justify a score near 15 despite the genuine practical merits.
